Supervised Learning

The matrix formulation of both feed-foward neural networks and convolutional neural networks (and other networks as well, for example, transformers) is inspired by the linear relationship between the parameters of the network. However, when the dimensions of the space the parameters live in begins to grow, and so do the relationships between parameters, matrices become an inappropriate tool to mathematically describe the model and a rather clumsy tool to describe the backpropogation algorithm, so here, tensors are chosen instead. Tensors arive when the sample space needs multiple numbers to index the basis, such as in the case of image data. The first part of the article deals with classical feed-forward networks, where the data is assumed to be linearized, so tensors won't make their appearance there. The second section however deals with convolutional nets, which do deal with higher dimensional data. Tensors aren't technically required to formally talk about such data; all one needs really is a multiindex-able object, say something like Ra×b×…\reals^{a \times b \times \ldots}Ra×b×…. Infact these can be identified with tensors. Tensors are chosen because the machinery they come with makes alot of the derivations much cleaner.

1. Feed Forward Neural Networks

We will call a neural network a layered model that produces features of samples in a "linear" way, by using parameters and the sample features at previous layers and then applying a non-linear transform. Define the following:
  • Dataset: D={{(xˉi)j}j≤J,vˉi}i≤I\mathcal{D} = \{\{(\bar{x}^i)^{j}\}_{j \leq J}, \bar{v}^i\}_{i \leq I}D={{(xˉi)j}j≤J​,vˉi}i≤I​ for some I∈NI \in \Bbb{N}I∈N where (xi)j∈R(x^i)^{j} \in \mathbb{R}(xi)j∈R is the jth feature of sample iii and vi∈Rv^i \in \mathbb{R}vi∈R is its label
  • The jjjth feature of the iiith sample produced at hidden layer l−1l-1l−1, feeding into hidden layer lll. (yi,l−1)j(y^{i,l-1})^{j}(yi,l−1)j
Suppose now we have (yi,l−1)j(y^{i,l-1})^{j}(yi,l−1)j for every j≤Jlj \leq J_lj≤Jl​. We aim to produce [one of] the next features (yi,l)k(y^{i, l})^{k}(yi,l)k for the same sample iii; namely feature number k≤Kl=Jl+1k \leq K_l=J_{l+1}k≤Kl​=Jl+1​ not necessarily equal to jjj. The feed-forward neural network (FFN) achieves this in two steps:
  1. We take a set of parameters {(Wl)j,k,(bl)k∈R}j≤Jl,k≤Kl=Jl+1\{(W^l)^{j,k}, (b^l)^k \in \Bbb{R}\}_{j \leq J_l, k \leq K_l=J_{l+1}}{(Wl)j,k,(bl)k∈R}j≤Jl​,k≤Kl​=Jl+1​​ - we may also call these weights and biases - and multiply each to the respective jjjth feature of yi,l−1y^{i, l-1}yi,l−1 at layer l−1l-1l−1, before summing. That is, we produce (zi,l)k=∑j≤Jl(yi,l−1)j(Wl)j,k+(bl)k\begin{equation} (z^{i,l})^{k} = \sum_{j \leq J_l}(y^{i, l-1})^{j} (W^l)^{j,k} + (b^l)^k \end{equation}(zi,l)k=j≤Jl​∑​(yi,l−1)j(Wl)j,k+(bl)k​​ a "preimage" of the kkkth feature of the iiith sample at layer lll. Just the preimage thus far, since at step 2...
  2. a smooth, nonlinear transform from C∞(R,R)C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{R})C∞(R,R) is henceforth applied: (yi,l)k=fl((zi,l)k)\begin{equation} (y^{i,l})^{k} = f_l((z^{i,l})^{k}) \end{equation}(yi,l)k=fl​((zi,l)k)​​ producing the desired feature.

Tensors

It is at this point we will specify important details needed to understand the rest of the article. Firstly, we will use Einstein's Summation Convention (ESC) to simplify sums with a repeated index, signifying the summation of the terms over said index. For example, we can rewrite (1) as (zi,l)k=(yi,l−1)j(Wl)j,k+bk\begin{equation} (z^{i,l})^{k} = (y^{i,l-1})^{j} (W^l)^{j,k} + b^k \end{equation}(zi,l)k=(yi,l−1)j(Wl)j,k+bk​​ where the sum is meant to be over jjj, which repeats, and where all terms are zero outside of their domains. This too deserves formalization. Firstly, let's consider (yi,l)(y^{i,l})(yi,l) as a well defined object, namely, a tensor over infinite dimensional vector spaces, but with finite support. Let's clarify, fix a feature tensor at layer lll: yi,l=(yi,l)jej∈Vy^{i,l} = (y^{i,l})^{j} e_j \in \Bbb{V}yi,l=(yi,l)jej​∈V Importantly, this is just a vector. However we are going to blur the distinction to warm up he reader to tensors, since this can be considered a tensor with a single slot. Let's also define what samples are xi=(xi)jej∈Vx^i = (x^i)^j e_j \in \Bbb{V}xi=(xi)jej​∈V again, using ESC. Now we can define the other objects we'll use xˉ=∏i(xˉi)jej∈∏iVvˉ=∑ivˉiei∈RIWl=(Wl)j,kej⊗ek∈V⊗Vbl=(bl)kek∈V\begin{align} \bar{\bm{x}} &= \prod_i (\bar{x}^{i})^{j} e_j &&\in \prod_i \Bbb{V} \\ \bar{\bm{v}} &= \sum_i \bar{v}^i e_i &&\in \mathbb{R}^{I}\\ W^l &= (W^l)^{j,k} e_j \otimes e_k &&\in \Bbb{V} \otimes \Bbb{V} \\ b^l &= (b^l)^{k} e_k &&\in \Bbb{V} \end{align}xˉvˉWlbl​=i∏​(xˉi)jej​=i∑​vˉiei​=(Wl)j,kej​⊗ek​=(bl)kek​​​∈i∏​V∈RI∈V⊗V∈V​​
Throughout the article, V=RZ\mathbb{V} = \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{Z}}V=RZ and V⊗2=V⊗V\mathbb{V}^{\otimes 2} = \mathbb{V} \otimes \mathbb{V}V⊗2=V⊗V
We also need to transform the R→R\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}R→R transform into a V→V\Bbb{V}\to \Bbb{V}V→V transform that acts on tensors, by defining yi,l=Fl(zi,l)=fl((zi,l)k)ek\begin{equation} y^{i,l} = F_l(z^{i,l}) = f_l((z^{i,l})^{k}) e_k \end{equation}yi,l=Fl​(zi,l)=fl​((zi,l)k)ek​​​ We will also make use of Abstract Index Notation (AIN), which is particularly useful when representing the shape of a tensor. For example, we could write (yl)ab(y_l)^{ab}(yl​)ab to denote that yl∈V⊗Vy_l \in V \otimes Vyl​∈V⊗V, or for a more general example TabcdeT^{ab}{}_{c}{}^{d}{}_{e}Tabc​de​ to denote a tensor T∈V⊗V⊗V∗⊗V⊗V∗T \in V \otimes V \otimes V^* \otimes V \otimes V^*T∈V⊗V⊗V∗⊗V⊗V∗.

Contraction, Inner Products, Metric Tensors


The issue thus far is that we want to speak in a language of tensors and yet are using the coefficients of the layer features and parameters. Using basic linear algebra, one realizes that zi,lz^{i,l}zi,l can be formulated as a matrix product, where the inner product is over the space indexed by jjj. Using tensors however, we see it as the image of the metric tensor, or, if one of the jjj were lowered, as a contraction. Before jumping in, we need to agree on contraction notation; in (AIN) this is straighforward:
Let Sab=Sijei⊗ejS^{a}{}_{b} = S^i{}_j e_i \otimes e^jSab​=Sij​ei​⊗ej be arbitrary. Contraction along slots a,ba,ba,b is defined as Saa=Sijej(ei)S^{a}{}_{a} = S^i{}_j e^j(e_i)Saa​=Sij​ej(ei​) In the case where ej(ei)=δije^j(e_i) = \delta_{ij}ej(ei​)=δij​: Sab=SiiS^{a}{}_{b} = S^i{}_iSab​=Sii​ which using ESC is just the sum of the diagonal indices.
We should talk briefly about the metric tensor gabg_{ab}gab​ and the inverse metric tensor gab{g}^{ab}gab. V\Bbb{V}V has the canonical orthonormal basis {ei}\{e_i \}{ei​}, and is endowed with the canonical inner product ⟨ei,ej⟩=δij\langle e_i , e_j \rangle = \delta_{ij}⟨ei​,ej​⟩=δij​. Such an inner product admits a dual basis for V∗\Bbb{V}^*V∗ defined by {ei=⟨⋅,ei⟩}\{e^i = \langle \cdot, e_i \rangle\}{ei=⟨⋅,ei​⟩}. The metric tensors are then given by agreement with the inner products gab=gi,jei⊗ej=δijei⊗ejgab=gi,jei⊗ej=δijei⊗ej\begin{align} g_{ab} = g_{i,j} e^i \otimes e^j = \delta_{ij} e^i \otimes e^j \\ {g}^{ab} = g^{i,j} e_i \otimes e_j = \delta_{ij} e_i \otimes e_j \end{align}gab​=gi,j​ei⊗ej=δij​ei⊗ejgab=gi,jei​⊗ej​=δij​ei​⊗ej​​​ Now we can now show contraction against the metric ggg
gabSaTb=δijSpei(ep)Tqej(eq)=SiTig_{ab} S^{a} T^{b} = \delta_{ij} S^p e^i(e_p) T^q e^j(e_q) = S^i T^igab​SaTb=δij​Spei(ep​)Tqej(eq​)=SiTi gabSaTb=δijSpep(ei)Tqeq(ej)=SiTig^{ab} S_{a} T_{b} = \delta_{ij} S_p e^p(e_i) T_q e^q(e_j) = S_i T_igabSa​Tb​=δij​Sp​ep(ei​)Tq​eq(ej​)=Si​Ti​ A [very] useful property is that the metric tensors can raise/lower indices. For example, gabva=δijei⊗ej(vpep)=viei=vag_{ab} v^a = \delta_{ij} e^i \otimes e^j(v^p e_p) = v^i e^i = v_agab​va=δij​ei⊗ej(vpep​)=viei=va​ It should be understood that if vav_ava​ is given when vav^ava was defined, the index has been moved via application of a metric tensor.
Now we can find a suitable tensorial representation for zi,lz^{i,l}zi,l:
zi,l=(yi,l−1)a(Wl)ab+blz^{i,l} = (y^{i,l-1})_{a}(W^l)^{ab} + b^lzi,l=(yi,l−1)a​(Wl)ab+bl

The Model

We now formalize the FNN model F\mathcal{F}F completely.

  • We will call a layer l=1...Ll=1...Ll=1...L the function yi,l−1↦Ll(yi,l−1;Wl,bl)=Fl∘Γl(yi,l−1,Wl,bl)y^{i,l-1} \mapsto \mathcal{L}_l(y^{i,l-1} ; W^l, b^l) = F_l \circ \Gamma_l(y^{i,l-1}, W^l, b^l)yi,l−1↦Ll​(yi,l−1;Wl,bl)=Fl​∘Γl​(yi,l−1,Wl,bl) where Γl(Sa,Tab,Ua)=SaTab+Ua\begin{equation} \Gamma_{l}(S^a,T^{ab},U^{a}) = S_{a}T^{ab}+ U^a \end{equation}Γl​(Sa,Tab,Ua)=Sa​Tab+Ua​​ We will call the neuron kkk at layer lll the function yi,l−1↦Nl,k(yi,l−1;(Wl)j,kej,(bl)k)=Fl∘γl(yi,l−1,(Wl)j,kej,(bl)k)y^{i,l-1} \mapsto \mathcal{N}_{l,k}(y^{i,l-1} ; (W^l)^{j,k} e_j , (b^l)^k) = F_l \circ \gamma_{l}(y^{i,l-1}, (W^l)^{j,k} e_j, (b^l)^k)yi,l−1↦Nl,k​(yi,l−1;(Wl)j,kej​,(bl)k)=Fl​∘γl​(yi,l−1,(Wl)j,kej​,(bl)k) where γl(Sa,Ta,u)=SaTa+u\gamma_{l}(S^a,T^a, u) = S_{a}T^{a}+ uγl​(Sa,Ta,u)=Sa​Ta+u Note that Nl,k(yi,l−1;(Wl)j,kej,(bl)k)ek=Ll(yi,l−1;Wl,bl)\mathcal{N}_{l,k}(y^{i,l-1} ; (W^l)^{j,k} e_j , (b^l)^k) e_k = \mathcal{L}_l(y^{i,l-1}; W^l, b^l)Nl,k​(yi,l−1;(Wl)j,kej​,(bl)k)ek​=Ll​(yi,l−1;Wl,bl) that is, a layer is a sum of neurons.
  • First we start with the input layer , L0\mathcal{L}_0L0​. We define yi,0:=xiy^{i,0} := x^iyi,0:=xi for any sample xi∈Vx^i \in \Bbb{V}xi∈V and define L0\mathcal{L}_0L0​ by xi↦yi,0x^i \mapsto y^{i,0}xi↦yi,0, so L0\mathcal{L}_0L0​ is the identity. It's not strictly a computational layer like defined earlier, however some folks like to speak of an input layer, which refers to this.
  • The hidden layers are {Ll}l=1…L\{\mathcal{L}_l\}_{ l=1\dots L}{Ll​}l=1…L​
  • The output layer is yi,L↦LL+1(yi,L;WL+1,bL+1)=FL+1∘Γ(yi,L,WL+1,bL+1)y^{i,L} \mapsto \mathcal{L}_{L+1}(y^{i,L}; W^{L+1}, b^{L+1}) = F_{L+1} \circ \Gamma(y^{i,L}, W^{L+1}, b^{L+1})yi,L↦LL+1​(yi,L;WL+1,bL+1)=FL+1​∘Γ(yi,L,WL+1,bL+1) where FL+1F_{L+1}FL+1​ is called the activation function.
  • The model F\mathcal{F}F is defined by F(x;θ)=LL+1(⋅;WL+1,bL+1)∘…∘L1(⋅;W1,b1)∘L0(x)\mathcal{F}(x ; \theta) = \mathcal{L}_{L+1}(\cdot ; W^{L+1},b^{L+1}) \circ \ldots \circ \mathcal{L}_{1}(\cdot ; W^{1}, b^1) \circ \mathcal{L_0} (x)F(x;θ)=LL+1​(⋅;WL+1,bL+1)∘…∘L1​(⋅;W1,b1)∘L0​(x) where θ=W1,b1…WL+1,bL+1\theta = W_1,b_1 \ldots W_{L+1},b_{L+1}θ=W1​,b1​…WL+1​,bL+1​ are the parameters of the model.

Loss, Empirical Risk

We have so far the ability to compute the output of our parameterized model yi,L+1=F(xi;θ)y^{i,L+1} = \mathcal{F}(x^i;\theta)yi,L+1=F(xi;θ).

Let X,YX,YX,Y be the random variables for input features and labels, over the spaces X,Y\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}X,Y. Let X,Y∼P(X,Y)X,Y \sim \mathcal{P}(X,Y)X,Y∼P(X,Y) with pdf pX,Y(x,y)p_{X,Y}(x,y)pX,Y​(x,y). Let Xi,YiX_i,Y_iXi​,Yi​ be the ith feature and label random variables, and assume Xi,Yi∼i.i.dP(X,Y)X_i, Y_i \sim_{i.i.d} \mathcal{P}(X,Y)Xi​,Yi​∼i.i.d​P(X,Y) Define a loss function R×V→R:\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{V} \to \mathbb{R}:R×V→R: w,w^↦Δ(w,w^)w, \hat{w} \mapsto \Delta(w, \hat{w})w,w^↦Δ(w,w^) Define T[i]=∑αTi,αei⊗eαT⟩i⟨=∑αTi,αeαT⟨i⟩=∑αTαei⊗eα=ei⊗T\begin{align*} T^{[i]} &= \sum_{\alpha} T^{i,\alpha} e_i \otimes e_{\alpha} \\ T^{\rangle i \langle} &= \sum_{\alpha} T^{i,\alpha} e_{\alpha} \\ T^{\langle i \rangle}& = \sum_{\alpha} T^{\alpha} e_i \otimes e_{\alpha} = e_i \otimes T \end{align*}T[i]T⟩i⟨T⟨i⟩​=α∑​Ti,αei​⊗eα​=α∑​Ti,αeα​=α∑​Tαei​⊗eα​=ei​⊗T​ The loss at a point (x,y)∈V×R(x,y) \in \mathbb{V} \times \mathbb{R}(x,y)∈V×R is l(x,y,h)=Δ(y,h(x))l(x, y,h) = \Delta(y, h(x))l(x,y,h)=Δ(y,h(x)) The risk is the expected value of the loss over X×Y\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}X×Y R(h)=EX,Y(l(x,y,h))=∫l(x,y,h)pX,Y(x,y)dxdyR(h) = \mathbb{E}_{X,Y}(l(x,y,h)) = \int l(x,y,h) p_{X,Y}(x,y) dxdyR(h)=EX,Y​(l(x,y,h))=∫l(x,y,h)pX,Y​(x,y)dxdy which is intractable, so the empirical risk over a sample d=(x,y)\bm{d}=( \bm{x}, \bm{y})d=(x,y) is used instead, which, as data size grows, converges to the risk by the LLN: R^(d,h)=1I∑il(xi,yi,h)→EX,Y(l(x,y,h))\begin{equation} \hat{R}(\bm{d}, h) = \frac{1}{I}\sum_i l(x_i,y_i,h) \to \mathbb{E}_{X,Y}(l(x,y,h)) \end{equation}R^(d,h)=I1​i∑​l(xi​,yi​,h)→EX,Y​(l(x,y,h))​​as I→∞I\to\inftyI→∞. Empirical Risk Minimization chooses a model space H\mathcal{H}H and finds arg min⁡h∈HR^(d,h)\argmin_{h \in \mathcal{H}}\hat{R}(\bm{d}, h)h∈Hargmin​R^(d,h)
For our purposes, X=V,Y=R\mathcal{X}=\Bbb{V}, \mathcal{Y}=\Bbb{R}X=V,Y=R. Our loss is defined as l(xi,vi,F(⋅;θ))=Δ(v,F(xi;θ))l(x^i, v^i, \mathcal{F}(\cdot; \theta)) = \Delta(v, \mathcal{F}(x^i;\theta))l(xi,vi,F(⋅;θ))=Δ(v,F(xi;θ)) and for a sample d=(x,v)\bm{d} = (\bm{x}, \bm{v})d=(x,v) R^(d,F(⋅;θ))=1I∑il(xi,vi,F(⋅;θ))→EX,Y(l(x,v,F(⋅;θ)))\hat{R}(\bm{d}, \mathcal{F}(\cdot; \theta)) = \frac{1}{I}\sum_i l(x^i, v^i, \mathcal{F}(\cdot; \theta)) \to \Bbb{E}_{X, Y}(l(x, v, \mathcal{F}(\cdot; \theta)))R^(d,F(⋅;θ))=I1​i∑​l(xi,vi,F(⋅;θ))→EX,Y​(l(x,v,F(⋅;θ)))
So given our sample dˉ=(xˉ,vˉ)\bar{\bm{d}} = (\bar{\bm{x}}, \bar{\bm{v}})dˉ=(xˉ,vˉ) we find arg min⁡θR^(dˉ,F(⋅;θ))=arg min⁡θ1I∑il(xi,vˉi,F(⋅;θ))=arg min⁡θ1I∑iΔ(vˉi,F(xˉi;θ))\argmin_{\theta} \hat{R}(\bar{\bm{d}}, \mathcal{F}(\cdot ; \theta)) = \argmin_{\theta}\frac{1}{I}\sum_i l(x^i,\bar{v}^i, \mathcal{F}(\cdot; \theta)) \\ = \argmin_{\theta}\frac{1}{I}\sum_i \Delta(\bar{v}^i, \mathcal{F}(\bar{x}^i; \theta))θargmin​R^(dˉ,F(⋅;θ))=θargmin​I1​i∑​l(xi,vˉi,F(⋅;θ))=θargmin​I1​i∑​Δ(vˉi,F(xˉi;θ))

Loss Function, Activation Functions

We will need a way to choose the loss function Δ\DeltaΔ. While we could make an arbitrary choice, we could also use Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) to derive it. Let P={P(X,Y;θ):pX,Y(x,y;θ)=pY∣X(y∣x;θ)pX(x)=p0(y;F(x;θ))pX(x)}θ∈Θ\mathscr{P}=\{\mathcal{P}(X,Y; \theta) : p_{X,Y}(x,y;\theta) = p_{Y|X}(y|x;\theta)p_X(x) = p_0(y;\mathcal{F}(x;\theta))p_X(x) \}_{\theta \in \Theta }P={P(X,Y;θ):pX,Y​(x,y;θ)=pY∣X​(y∣x;θ)pX​(x)=p0​(y;F(x;θ))pX​(x)}θ∈Θ​ and assume X,Y∼P(X,Y;θ)∈PX,Y \sim \mathcal{P}(X, Y; {\theta}) \in \mathscr{P}X,Y∼P(X,Y;θ)∈P with density pX,Y(x,y;θ)=p0(y;F(x;θ))pX(x)p_{X,Y}(x,y;\theta) = p_0(y;\mathcal{F}(x;\theta))p_X(x)pX,Y​(x,y;θ)=p0​(y;F(x;θ))pX​(x) for some θ\thetaθ. The sample distribution for the random vector D=(X,Y){\bf D}= ({\bf X}, {\bf Y})D=(X,Y) is then given by the density pD(d;θ)=i.i.d∏ip(xi,yi;θ)=∏ip0(yi;F(xi;θ))pX(xi)p_{{\bf D}}(\bm{d};\theta)=_{i.i.d} \prod_i p(x^i, y^i;\theta) = \prod_i p_0(y^i;\mathcal{F}(x^i;\theta))p_X(x^i)pD​(d;θ)=i.i.d​i∏​p(xi,yi;θ)=i∏​p0​(yi;F(xi;θ))pX​(xi)
With our X=V,Y=R\mathcal{X} = \Bbb{V}, \mathcal{Y} = \Bbb{R}X=V,Y=R and d=x,v\bm{d} = \bm{x}, \bm{v}d=x,v pD(d;θ)=∏ip0(vi;F(xi;θ))pX(xi)p_{\bf D} (\bm{d}; \theta)= \prod_i p_0(v^i;\mathcal{F}(x^i;\theta))p_X(x^i)pD​(d;θ)=i∏​p0​(vi;F(xi;θ))pX​(xi)
The likelihood is L(θ;dˉ)=pD(dˉ;θ)=∏ip0(vˉi;F(xˉi;θ))pX(xˉi)\mathbb{L}(\theta; \bar{\bm{d}}) = p_{\bf D}(\bar{\bm{d}}; \theta) = \prod_i p_0(\bar{v}^i;\mathcal{F}(\bar{x}^i;\theta))p_X(\bar{x}^i)L(θ;dˉ)=pD​(dˉ;θ)=i∏​p0​(vˉi;F(xˉi;θ))pX​(xˉi) Taking the negative log gives −log⁡(L(θ;dˉ))=−∑ilog⁡(pX(xˉi))−∑ilog⁡(p0(vˉi;F(xˉi;θ)))-\log(\mathbb{L}(\theta; \bm{\bar{d}})) = -\sum_i \log(p_X(\bar{x}^i)) - \sum_i \log(p_0(\bar{v}^i;\mathcal{F}(\bar{x}^{i}; \theta)))−log(L(θ;dˉ))=−i∑​log(pX​(xˉi))−i∑​log(p0​(vˉi;F(xˉi;θ))) which we want minimized over θ\thetaθ. In practice, it's helpful to vectorize along the batch sample because the partial derivatives will be more computationally efficient to work with. Adjunction

The gradient is technically the adjoint of the derivative ∇f(x)=(Df(x))†\nabla f(x) = (Df(x))^{\dagger}∇f(x)=(Df(x))† Since we will express all derivatives as tensors, we need to quickly mention the suitable 'adjunction' operator for tensors: if T∈Hom(V,W)T \in \text{Hom}(V, W)T∈Hom(V,W) where VVV has basis {eI}\{e_{\mathcal{I}}\}{eI​}, WWW has basis {fI}\{f_{\mathcal{I}}\}{fI​}, and both spaces are endowed with the standard products ⟨eI,eJ⟩=δI,J\langle e_{\mathcal{I}}, e_{\mathcal{J}}\rangle = \delta_{\mathcal{I}, \mathcal{J}}⟨eI​,eJ​⟩=δI,J​ and ⟨fI,fJ⟩=δI,J\langle f_{\mathcal{I}}, f_{\mathcal{J}}\rangle = \delta_{\mathcal{I}, \mathcal{J}}⟨fI​,fJ​⟩=δI,J​ , and V∗,W∗V^*, W^*V∗,W∗ have the dual bases induced from these inner products, then ϕ(T†)=⟨fJ,T(eI)⟩eI⊗fJ\phi(T^{\dagger}) = \langle f_{\mathcal{J}}, T(e_{\mathcal{I}}) \rangle e_{\mathcal{I}} \otimes f^{\mathcal{J}}ϕ(T†)=⟨fJ​,T(eI​)⟩eI​⊗fJ Also ϕ(T)=T(eI)⊗eI=⟨fJ,T(eI)⟩fJ⊗eI\phi(T) = T(e_{\mathcal{I}}) \otimes e^{\mathcal{I}} \\ = \langle f_{\mathcal{J}}, T(e_{\mathcal{I}}) \rangle f_{\mathcal{J}} \otimes e^{\mathcal{I}}ϕ(T)=T(eI​)⊗eI=⟨fJ​,T(eI​)⟩fJ​⊗eI Thus 'adunction' on tensors can be defined by

The Gradients

In practice, solving for θ∗=arg min⁡R^(dˉ;F(⋅;θ))\theta^* = \argmin \hat{R}(\bar{\bm{d}}; \mathcal{F}(\cdot; \theta))θ∗=argminR^(dˉ;F(⋅;θ)) is infeasible for many reasons, two important ones being the many flat regions of the objective R^\hat{R}R^ and the large matrix inversions that would have to be computed. The procedure to find the gradients will be illustrated. Note that transposition is used to denote permuting the slots of 2-tensors.

The machinery used to formalize FNNs is even more applicable to convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Perturb WlcW^c_lWlc​: ∂2Γlc(yl−1c,Wlc,blc)=dWlc↦yl−1c⋊dWlc  ⟹  ϕ(∂2Γlc(yl−1c,Wlc,blc))=(yl−1c⋊eαβγδ)⊗eαβγδ=(yl−1c)ituvτ(eαβγδ;(s,r))jtuveijsr⊗eαβγδ=(yl−1c)ituvτ(eαβγδ;(s,r))jtuveijsr⊗eαβγδ=(yl−1c)ituv(eαβ(γ+s)(δ+r))jtuveijsr⊗eαβγδ=(yl−1c)iβ(γ+s)(δ+r)eiαsr⊗eαβγδ\begin{align*} \partial_{2}\Gamma_l^c({\bf y}_{l-1}^c, W_l^c, b_l^c) &= dW^c_l \mapsto y^c_{l-1} \rtimes dW^c_l \\ \implies \phi(\partial_{2}\Gamma_l^c({\bf y}_{l-1}^c, W_l^c, b_l^c)) &= (y^c_{l-1} \rtimes e_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}) \otimes e^{\alpha \beta\gamma\delta} \\ &= (y^c_{l-1})^{ituv} \tau(e_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}; (s, r))^{jtuv} e_{ijsr} \otimes e^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta} \\ &= (y^c_{l-1})^{ituv} \tau(e_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}; (s, r))^{jtuv} e_{ijsr} \otimes e^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta} \\ &= (y^c_{l-1})^{ituv} (e_{\alpha\beta(\gamma+s)(\delta+r)})^{jtuv} e_{ijsr} \otimes e^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta} \\ &= (y^c_{l-1})^{i\beta(\gamma+s)(\delta+r)} e_{i\alpha sr} \otimes e^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta} \\ \end{align*}∂2​Γlc​(yl−1c​,Wlc​,blc​)⟹ϕ(∂2​Γlc​(yl−1c​,Wlc​,blc​))​=dWlc​↦yl−1c​⋊dWlc​=(yl−1c​⋊eαβγδ​)⊗eαβγδ=(yl−1c​)ituvτ(eαβγδ​;(s,r))jtuveijsr​⊗eαβγδ=(yl−1c​)ituvτ(eαβγδ​;(s,r))jtuveijsr​⊗eαβγδ=(yl−1c​)ituv(eαβ(γ+s)(δ+r)​)jtuveijsr​⊗eαβγδ=(yl−1c​)iβ(γ+s)(δ+r)eiαsr​⊗eαβγδ​
QED
ϕ(∂3Γlc(yl−1c,Wlc,blc))=1a⊗eα⊗1bc⊗eα\phi(\partial_{3}\Gamma_l^c({\bf y}_{l-1}^c, W_l^c, b_l^c) ) = \bm{1}^{a} \otimes e_{\alpha} \otimes \bm{1}^{bc} \otimes e^{\alpha}ϕ(∂3​Γlc​(yl−1c​,Wlc​,blc​))=1a⊗eα​⊗1bc⊗eα

The Gradients

Define the following: ξl=ϕ(∂1Ulc(ylc,θ))=(ξlc)tuvwetuvwξz=ϕ(∂1Ulc(ylc,θ)∘DFlc(zlc))δw=ϕ(∂WlcR^(dˉ;F(⋅;θ)))δb=ϕ(∂blcR^(dˉ;F(⋅;θ)))ϵw=ϕ(∂WlcΓlc(yl−1,θlc))=(yl−1c)iβ(γ+s)(δ+r)eiαsr⊗eαβγδϵb=ϕ(∂blcΓlc(yl−1,θlc))=1a⊗eα⊗1bc⊗eαϵz=ϕ(DFlc(zlc))=flc′((zlc)ijmn)⊗eijmn⊗eijmnϵl−1=ϕ(∂1Γlc(yl−1;θlc))=(Wlc)jβ(γ−s)(δ−r)eαjsr⊗eαβγδ\begin{align*} {\bm{\xi}}_l{} &= \phi(\partial_{1} U^c_l{}({\bf y}^c_l{}, \theta)) &= ({\xi}^c_l{})_{tuvw} e^{tuvw}\\ {\bm{\xi}}_z &= \phi(\partial_{1} U^c_l{}({\bf y}^c_l{}, \theta) \circ DF^c_l{}({\bf z}^c_l{})) \\ {\bm{\delta}}_w &= \phi(\partial_{W^c_l{}} \hat{R}(\bar{\bm{d}}; \mathcal{F}(\cdot; \theta))) \\ {\bm{\delta}}_b &= \phi(\partial_{b^c_l{}} \hat{R}(\bar{\bm{d}}; \mathcal{F}(\cdot; \theta)))\\ \bm{\epsilon}_w &= \phi(\partial_{W^c_l{}}\Gamma^c_l{}({\bf y}_{l-1}, \theta^c_l{})) &= (y^c_{l-1})^{i\beta(\gamma+s)(\delta+r)} e_{i\alpha sr} \otimes e^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}\\ \bm{\epsilon}_b &= \phi(\partial_{b^c_l{}}\Gamma^c_l{}({\bf y}_{l-1}, \theta^c_l{})) &= \bm{1}^{a} \otimes e_{\alpha} \otimes \bm{1}^{bc} \otimes e^{\alpha} \\ \bm{\epsilon}_z &= \phi(DF^c_l{}({\bf z}^c_l{})) & = f^{c}_l{}'((z^c_l)^{ijmn}) \otimes e_{ijmn} \otimes e^{ijmn} \\ \bm{\epsilon}_{l-1} &= \phi(\partial_{1} \Gamma^c_l{}({\bf y}_{l-1}; \theta^c_l{})) &= (W^c_l)^{j\beta (\gamma-s)(\delta-r)} e_{\alpha jsr} \otimes e^{\alpha \beta \gamma \delta} \\ \end{align*}ξl​ξz​δw​δb​ϵw​ϵb​ϵz​ϵl−1​​=ϕ(∂1​Ulc​(ylc​,θ))=ϕ(∂1​Ulc​(ylc​,θ)∘DFlc​(zlc​))=ϕ(∂Wlc​​R^(dˉ;F(⋅;θ)))=ϕ(∂blc​​R^(dˉ;F(⋅;θ)))=ϕ(∂Wlc​​Γlc​(yl−1​,θlc​))=ϕ(∂blc​​Γlc​(yl−1​,θlc​))=ϕ(DFlc​(zlc​))=ϕ(∂1​Γlc​(yl−1​;θlc​))​=(ξlc​)tuvw​etuvw=(yl−1c​)iβ(γ+s)(δ+r)eiαsr​⊗eαβγδ=1a⊗eα​⊗1bc⊗eα=flc​′((zlc​)ijmn)⊗eijmn​⊗eijmn=(Wlc​)jβ(γ−s)(δ−r)eαjsr​⊗eαβγδ​ By the preceding work we can find the gradient tensors for each parameter. NOTE: all transpositions denote permuting the first two slots.

Proof
δw=ϕ(∂1Ulc(ylc,θ)∘DFlc(zlc)∘∂WlcΓlc(yl−1,θlc))=(ξz)abcd(ϵw)abcdefgh=(ξz)tuvw(yl−1c)tβ(γ+v)(δ+w)euβγδ  ⟹  δw†=(ξz)tuvw(yl−1c)tβ(γ+v)(δ+w)euβγδ=(ξz†T)utvw(yl−1cT)βt(γ+v)(δ+w)euβγδ=ξzT⋉yl−1cT≡(yl−1cT⋊ξzT)T\begin{align*} \bm{\delta}_w &= \phi \left( \partial_{1} U^c_l{}({\bf y}^c_l{}, \theta) \circ DF^c_l{}({\bf z}^c_l{}) \circ \partial_{W^c_l{}}\Gamma^c_l{}({\bf y}_{l-1}, \theta^c_l{}) \right) \\ &= (\bm{\xi}_z){}_{abcd} (\bm{\epsilon}_w)^{abcd}{}_{efgh} \\ &= (\xi_z)_{tuvw} (y^c_{l-1})^{t\beta(\gamma+v)(\delta+w)} e^{u\beta\gamma\delta}\\ \implies \bm{\delta}_w^{\dagger} &= (\xi_z)_{tuvw} (y^c_{l-1})^{t\beta(\gamma+v)(\delta+w)} e_{u\beta\gamma\delta} \\ &= (\xi^{\dagger}_z{}^T)^{utvw} (y^c_{l-1}{}^T)^{\beta t(\gamma+v)(\delta+w)} e_{u\beta\gamma\delta} \\ &= \bm{\xi}^T_z \ltimes {\bf y}^c_{l-1}{}^T \\ &\equiv ({\bf y}^c_{l-1}{}^T \rtimes \bm{\xi}^T_z)^T \\ \end{align*}δw​⟹δw†​​=ϕ(∂1​Ulc​(ylc​,θ)∘DFlc​(zlc​)∘∂Wlc​​Γlc​(yl−1​,θlc​))=(ξz​)abcd​(ϵw​)abcdefgh​=(ξz​)tuvw​(yl−1c​)tβ(γ+v)(δ+w)euβγδ=(ξz​)tuvw​(yl−1c​)tβ(γ+v)(δ+w)euβγδ​=(ξz†​T)utvw(yl−1c​T)βt(γ+v)(δ+w)euβγδ​=ξzT​⋉yl−1c​T≡(yl−1c​T⋊ξzT​)T​
QED

δb=ϕ(∂1Ulc(ylc,θ)∘DFlc(zlc)∘∂blcΓlc(yl−1,θlc))=(ξz)abcd(ϵb)abcde=∑tvw(ξz)tuvweu  ⟹  δb†=∑tvw(ξz)tuvweu=∑tvw(ξz†)tuvweu=1acd(ξz†)abcd\begin{align*} \bm{\delta}_b &= \phi \left( \partial_{1} U^c_l{}({\bf y}^c_l{}, \theta) \circ DF^c_l{}({\bf z}^c_l{}) \circ \partial_{b^c_l{}}\Gamma^c_l{}({\bf y}_{l-1}, \theta^c_l{}) \right) \\ &= (\bm{\xi}_z){}_{abcd} (\bm{\epsilon}_b)^{abcd}{}_{e} \\ &= \sum_{tvw} (\xi_z)_{tuvw} e^u \\ \implies \bm{\delta}_b^{\dagger} &= \sum_{tvw} (\xi_z)_{tuvw} e_u \\ &= \sum_{tvw} (\xi^{\dagger}_z)^{tuvw} e_u \\ &=\bm{1}_{acd}(\bm{\xi}^{\dagger}_z)^{abcd} \\ \end{align*}δb​⟹δb†​​=ϕ(∂1​Ulc​(ylc​,θ)∘DFlc​(zlc​)∘∂blc​​Γlc​(yl−1​,θlc​))=(ξz​)abcd​(ϵb​)abcde​=tvw∑​(ξz​)tuvw​eu=tvw∑​(ξz​)tuvw​eu​=tvw∑​(ξz†​)tuvweu​=1acd​(ξz†​)abcd​

Proof
ξl−1=ϕ(∂1Ul−1c(yl−1c,θ))=ϕ(∂1Ulc(ylc,θ)∘DFlc(zlc)∘∂1Γlc(yl−1c,θlc))=(ξl)abcd(ϵz)abcdefgh(ϵl−1)efghwxyz=(ξz)efgh(ϵl−1)efghwxyz=(ξz)tuvw(Wlc)uβ(γ−v)(δ−w)etβγδ  ⟹  ξl−1†=(ξz)tuvw(Wlc)uβ(γ−v)(δ−w)etβγδ=(ξz†)tuvw(WlcT)βu(γ−v)(δ−w)etβγδ=(ξz†)tuvwχ2(WlcT)βu(v−γ)(w−δ)etβγδ=ξz†⋊ˉWlcT\begin{align*} \bm{\xi}_{l-1} &= \phi(\partial_1 U^c_{l-1}({\bf y}^c_{l-1}, \theta)) = \phi(\partial_{1} U^c_{l}({\bf y}^c_{l}, \theta) \circ DF^c_{l}({\bf z}^c_{l}) \circ \partial_1 \Gamma^c_{l}({\bf y}^c_{l-1}, \theta^c_l{}))\\ &= (\bm{\xi}_l{})_{abcd} (\bm{\epsilon}_z)^{abcd}{}_{efgh} (\bm{\epsilon}_{l-1})^{efgh}{}_{wxyz}\\ &= (\bm{\xi}_z)_{efgh} (\bm{\epsilon}_{l-1})^{efgh}{}_{wxyz}\\ &= (\xi_z)_{tuvw} (W^c_l)^{u\beta (\gamma-v)(\delta-w)} e^{t\beta \gamma \delta} \\ \implies \bm{\xi}_{l-1}{}^{\dagger} & = (\xi_z)_{tuvw} (W^c_l)^{u\beta (\gamma-v)(\delta-w)} e_{t\beta \gamma \delta} \\ & = (\xi^{\dagger}_z{})^{tuvw} (W^c_l{}^T)^{\beta u(\gamma-v)(\delta-w)} e_{t\beta \gamma \delta} \\ & =(\xi^{\dagger}_z{})^{tuvw} \chi_2(W^c_l{}^T)^{\beta u(v-\gamma)(w-\delta)} e_{t\beta \gamma \delta} \\ & = \bm{\xi}^{\dagger}_z{} \bar{\rtimes} W^c_l{}^T \end{align*}ξl−1​⟹ξl−1​†​=ϕ(∂1​Ul−1c​(yl−1c​,θ))=ϕ(∂1​Ulc​(ylc​,θ)∘DFlc​(zlc​)∘∂1​Γlc​(yl−1c​,θlc​))=(ξl​)abcd​(ϵz​)abcdefgh​(ϵl−1​)efghwxyz​=(ξz​)efgh​(ϵl−1​)efghwxyz​=(ξz​)tuvw​(Wlc​)uβ(γ−v)(δ−w)etβγδ=(ξz​)tuvw​(Wlc​)uβ(γ−v)(δ−w)etβγδ​=(ξz†​)tuvw(Wlc​T)βu(γ−v)(δ−w)etβγδ​=(ξz†​)tuvwχ2​(Wlc​T)βu(v−γ)(w−δ)etβγδ​=ξz†​⋊ˉ​Wlc​T​

I hope this was an informative read; the backpropagation procedure is derived so often in a way that sweeps important concepts under the rug. Tensors are the natural objects for high dimensional data, so it's important to know how to actually use them when they appear in ML.
